newsitem.title: CANADA: Bank of Montreal forecasts robust Canadian economy.
newsitem.headline: Bank of Montreal forecasts robust Canadian economy.

text.p: Canada's economy is on track for robust growth in 1997, which should strengthen the currency, increase employment and reduce the federal budget deficit, the Bank of Montreal forecast on Wednesday.
Bank of Montreal Chief Economist Tim O'Neill made the forecasts to the St. John's Board of Trade Business Outlook 1997 Conference.

In a statement from the bank, O'Neill forecast Canada's gross domestic product will grow by about 3.5 percent this year and next, which should lead to increased job growth and a fall in the unemployment rate.

"We're forecasting well over 300,000 new jobs both this year and next year, compared to the under 200,000 created in 1996. This should help lower the unemployment rate from 9.7% to 9.1% by the end of 1997 and 8.6% by the fourth quarter of 1998," said O'Neill.

Stronger growth, combined with Canada's low inflation rate and falling budget deficits, will likely contribute to a stronger dollar over the next two years, O'Neill said. O'Neill predicted the Canadian dollar will appreciate to US$0.775 cents by the end of 1997 and rise further to US$0.80 by the end of next year.
"While a stronger dollar will put pressure on Canadian exporters, that will be offset to some extent by a low-cost environment, including only moderate wage increases," said O'Neill.

Stronger growth should result in a lower-than-expected federal budget deficit, O'Neill said. The bank expects that the federal deficit could be as low as C$16 billion, or 2.0 percent of GDP for fiscal 1996-97. That would be well under the government's target of C$24.3 billion, or 3.0 percent of GDP.

On the monetary policy front, O'Neill said he does not expect the Bank of Canada to further lower interest rates. The Bank of Canada cut short-term interest rates 11 times last year, bringing prime lending rates at chartered banks to 40-year lows. Recent strength in the Canadian dollar has spurred some speculation that interest rates could fall again.

"We expect the Bank of Canada to reduce some of the current stimulus in the economy, but not until the second half of the year. The slight shift in policy should see the bank rate increase a quarter percent before the end of 1997 and another quarter point in early 1998," said O'Neill.
Canada's bank rate, which is set at the top of the central bank's target range for the overnight lending rate, is now at 3.25 percent.
O'Neill also forecast that Newfoundland's economy will expand by 1.0-1.4 percent in 1997 compared to a drop of 3.0 percent in 1996.

The province's economy is poised for stronger long-term growth as it continues to reshape and diversify, said O'Neill. He forecast economic growth will be broadly based, coming from the resource sector, a gradual recovery in fisheries and continued expansion of the information technology industry.
